title: M³E: Continual Vision-and-Language Navigation via Mixture of Macro and Micro Experts
one_liner: A robot reads text instructions and camera images to navigate indoor spaces, but forgets how to handle old environments when learning new ones—this paper splits navigation reasoning into two levels so it can adapt without erasing what it already knows.
lead: A robot that learns to navigate by following text instructions and looking at camera images faces a core problem: when it learns new environments, it forgets how to handle old ones—like forgetting how to work in an office building after learning a home layout. This paper proposes splitting the robot's reasoning into two separate pathways: a high-level "what kind of space is this" reasoner (office, residential, outdoor) and a low-level "which wall objects matter for this instruction" reasoner, so each can adapt independently without wiping out the other.

paras: A robot learns to navigate by reading instructions like 'turn left at the red door' and looking at camera images. When it trains in a residential home, it gets good at that space: it learns which doors matter, which walls are walkable, what 'left' means in that lighting. Then it moves to an office building. As it trains on office images and instructions, the weights (the numbers that make up the robot's brain) slowly shift to match the office world. But after 500 office steps, the robot has often rewritten its old home knowledge—it now misinterprets residential hallways because the numbers that once worked there are gone. This is catastrophic forgetting.

A beginner might try fine-tuning: take the weights learned in the home, then just keep tweaking them for the office. But the same rewriting happens—new learning overwrites old. The core problem is that residential and office spaces are different enough that a single set of weights cannot serve both cleanly.

callout.html: Train separate expert modules for different scene types and perception tasks, then learn which expert to activate in each situation, using a momentum-based update that slows down how fast old experts change.

steps.text: Robot camera captures image; map its visual features (walls, objects, lighting).
Macro router reads scene features, outputs a weighted blend: 80% home-expert, 20% office-expert.
Micro router reads instruction text and image patch, selects which perception expert to trust this step.
Blend of selected experts predicts next action: go forward, turn, stop.
When training, nudge expert weights gently (momentum means old ones move slowly), so old expertise does not die.

paras: Instead of one set of weights for all scenes and tasks, the robot now maintains separate expert weights plus two routing networks. The macro router learns to identify scene type. The micro router learns to identify perception needs per instruction-image pair. The paper also adds momentum (a slowness constant) to weight updates so old experts do not flip abruptly.

hidden.name: How much each expert is used in new environments
paras: As the robot enters a new domain (office after home), some old experts become useless—they were only right for home scenes. The paper measures expert utility: for each expert module, how often does the current domain ask the macro or micro router to activate it? High utility means keep updating it; low utility means freeze it to preserve old capability.

The paper uses a momentum update strategy: compute how much each expert was selected in the new domain, then scale the weight update by that utility. High-utility experts update quickly; low-utility experts barely move, preserving their old expertise.

heat.caption: Darker means higher utility in new domain. Highlighted cells freeze to preserve old memory.

reads.html: In a new environment, some old experts are still needed (they light up again), so they update. Others were only for the last domain (dark), so training barely touches them—they stay frozen with their old knowledge.

Dynamic momentum updates: new weight becomes old weight plus a change scaled by how little that expert was used. Experts used often train normally; rarely-used experts barely move, preserving old knowledge.

paras: Forgetting happens because a single weight set must represent both scene strategies (how to navigate a residential hallway vs. an office corridor) and local perceptions (which objects matter, which walls block, how lighting affects doors). When these conflict, updating for one overwrites the other.

Splitting into macro and micro experts decouples these two problems. The macro router learns high-level strategy for each scene type: in a home, focus on intimate scale and furniture; in an office, focus on open plans and cubicles. The micro router learns perception: which instruction words link to which visual features. These can be learned mostly independently. When a new domain arrives, the macro router can route heavily to its best old expert (because scene reasoning transfers), while the micro router can create fresh perception experts for the new look. Meanwhile, momentum keeps low-utility old experts frozen, preserving their specialized knowledge.

The mechanism works in three steps: (1) macro routing identifies scene similarity (new office may look similar to old office expertise, so reuse it); (2) micro routing picks perception modules per step (because this instruction-image pair needs specific local reasoning); (3) momentum update protects experts that are not heavily used in the new domain—if an expert is rarely selected, its weights barely move, so it stays sharp for its old domain. The result: old capabilities survive because they are not forced to compete with new learning.

items.html: If the macro router only ever selects one expert, the other experts never train and become useless. The paper must ensure router diversity, e.g., by gently pushing the router to spread selections or adding small random noise to scores.
If momentum is set too high (old experts barely update), new domains may be forced into poorly-fitting old experts, degrading performance. Tuning is needed.

If a new domain looks different from all prior scenes (e.g., outdoor garden after only indoor training), the macro router may misclassify, routing to the wrong strategy expert, causing poor performance.
Setting utility-based momentum adaptively—fast for high-utility experts, slow for low—lets the robot preserve old domains while still adapting to new ones.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Train a robot agent on VLN instructions in a home-like simulated environment (e.g., apartment building), measuring accuracy on home navigation tasks. Then train it on an office-like environment (cubicles, conference rooms) for 500 steps. At each step, measure: (1) How well does it still navigate the home? (2) How well does it navigate the office? (3) Are both high, or does office training destroy home knowledge? The demo should show that without the paper's dual routers and momentum, home accuracy drops below 50%, while with the paper's method both stay above 80%.
demo.closing: The demo makes impossible to miss: one version forgets the home (home drops to 38%), the other learns both (both stay at 84%).
